issue: Can a district court consider non-retroactive First Step Act changes in sentencing law (such as the § 924(c) stacking amendments in FSA § 403) when deciding whether an extraordinary and compelling reason exists for a sentence reduction under 18 U.S.C. § 3582(c)(1)(A)?

sides.position: A district court may not treat non-retroactive changes in sentencing law as an extraordinary and compelling reason for a sentence reduction (categorical prohibition).
cases: United States v. Jarvis, 999 F.3d 442 (6th Cir. 2021)
United States v. McKinnie (6th Cir. 2022) (endorsing Jarvis as law of circuit)

sides.position: A district court may consider non-retroactive sentencing changes in its extraordinary-and-compelling analysis; there is no categorical prohibition. The opinion says the Third, Seventh, and Eighth Circuits align with the prohibition side, so the opinion's holding conflicts with them.
cases: United States v. Ruvalcaba, No. 21-1064 (1st Cir. 2022)
United States v. Owens, 996 F.3d 755 (6th Cir. 2021) (6th Cir. holding on this side, since displaced by McKinnie)

this_court: The First Circuit rejects a categorical prohibition and holds that district courts may consider non-retroactive changes in sentencing law.
quote: A panel has recently endorsed a decision that aligns the court with the Third, Seventh, and Eighth Circuits.
cite: United States v. Ruvalcaba, No. 21-1064P (1st Cir. 2022)
